source.title: How much do language models memorize?
source.authors: J. X. Morris; Chawin Sitawarin; Chuan Guo; Narine Kokhlikyan; G. Suh; Alexander M. Rush; Kamalika Chaudhuri; Saeed Mahloujifar

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own measurements of memorization capacity, membership inference, and loss versus dataset size, but it does not test the claimed power laws for held-out loss or compute-optimal allocation. Its membership-inference scaling law is a different outcome.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fit or test held-out-loss power laws, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token splits. Its loss-versus-dataset-size results show double descent around model capacity; its membership-inference F1 results and capacity estimates concern different measures and are recorded as findings that fit no listed version. The text also cites prior scaling-law work, which is not recorded as a result.
record.test_reason: The study measures memorization capacity, membership inference and extraction. It fits no power law to held-out loss and tests no compute-optimal allocation or extrapolation of loss. Its one loss result (Figs 3-4) shows test-loss double descent as small, deduplicated FineWeb sets are trained to saturation (10^6 steps) on 1.7M–19M-parameter models. That is a heavily repeated-data, data-bottlenecked overfitting regime, outside V1's condition that the other factors are not the bottleneck. It has no fitted curve against which a bend (V7) could be judged. Its 'scaling law' predicts membership-inference F1, a different construct. So no version is tested. The record's labels on V1 and V7 contradict its own T6 call and are dropped.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude GPT-family models store about 3.6 bits/parameter (3.5–4 depending on architecture and precision). They find models memorize until capacity fills and then generalize, with double descent beginning when data exceeds capacity. Extraction on large deduplicated sets converges to the test extraction rate, so it is attributable to generalization. Their sigmoidal MI law, fit on small models, extrapolates to 125M–1.5B models. It implies modern LLMs are trained on too much data for reliable loss-based MI on average datapoints.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures memorization capacity, membership inference, and loss behavior around dataset capacity; it does not use the original studies’ held-out-loss scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The capacity estimate varies with precision: the reported mean is 3.51 bits per parameter in bfloat16 and 3.83 in fp32. Loss behavior is reported to change around dataset-to-capacity ratios; the membership-inference fit is described as least accurate near predicted F1 0.75.

fits_no_version.finding: Test loss on FineWeb shows double descent in dataset size: generalization begins near 10^5 samples, when dataset information exceeds model capacity (models 1.7M–19.2M params, trained to saturation).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In repeated-small-data training, held-out loss vs dataset size shows double descent at the dataset-to-capacity ratio of about 1.

fits_no_version.finding: Memorization capacity of GPT-style models on uniform random data is 3.5–3.6 bits/parameter. The mean is 3.51 (bf16) vs 3.83 (fp32) across widths and depths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization capacity scales linearly with parameters at about 3.6 bits/parameter.

fits_no_version.finding: A sigmoidal law in capacity/|D| predicts loss-based MI F1 within about 1.5 points on 125M and 1.5B models. The largest miss is at predicted 0.75 (65.69 observed for GPT2-Medium).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-based membership-inference F1 follows a sigmoid in the model-capacity-to-dataset-size ratio.

record.problems: The authors state that their results are specific to the tested environment and may not generalize to other datasets, architectures, or training setups. The loss curves do not report numerical fit parameters or uncertainty. The study does not test held-out-loss power-law fits or compute-optimal allocation.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified per-model loss values were stated in the text; Figures 3 and 4 show separate curves, so the loss result is recorded as the authors’ aggregate textual description in R1. Other figure-only membership-inference and extraction curve values are not recorded because the study’s stated results are summarized by the fitted relationship and Table 2.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss in parameters, tokens or compute, and no non-bottleneck regime.
Loss extrapolation not tested. Only the MI-F1 law is extrapolated, to 125M/1.5B models.
Widths and depths are varied only for memorization capacity (Table 1), not loss.
No other modality or regime tested for loss power laws.
No exponents fitted or compared, and no fitting-choice sensitivity for loss laws.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only for its architecture choice. Kaplan is an original source, but it is not tested here. The 'scaling laws' in the abstract concern membership inference, not pretraining loss.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies text dataset size and reports train/test loss behavior around model capacity, but does not fit power laws or test loss scaling with parameters or compute in a non-bottleneck regime.
The paper reports double descent in loss near model capacity, but does not compare fitted power-law exponents across setups, published laws, or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: text models (aggregate; parameter counts shown as 1,711,968, 3,620,544, 8,027,520, and 19,200,768)
rows.operation_detail: Trained models on text datasets of varying sizes and measured train and evaluation losses.

conditions.value: FineWeb text; training set size varied
dataset size varied relative to model capacity

rows.measure: Train and evaluation loss versus training set size
rows.value: The authors report double descent: evaluation loss decreases as training set size approaches model capacity, then rapidly drops once dataset capacity exceeds model capacity. Generalization begins at approximately 10^5 samples, depending on parameter count.
rows.note: Aggregate textual description of the results across the tested model sizes; the figures show separate curves, but no per-model values are given in the text.
rows.check: Linked to V1/V7, but it is test loss vs dataset size in a train-to-saturation, repeated-small-data regime, with no power-law fit and figure-only curves. It cannot show V1's power law in the non-bottleneck regime or V7's exponent/fit dependence. The value paraphrase also garbles the text, which says 'evaluation performance decreases… then rapidly drops'. Move it to fits_no_version.

rows.check: The fitted constants are the study's own model parameters, not a measured effect. The row is acceptable only as context for the MI law.
